The hierarchy is capital made visible. The Lords sit atop trade houses, factors and captains run their operations, and private security forces enforce contracts the courts are too slow to reach. Standing is measured in ships, warehouses, and outstanding debts owed to you, and it shifts with the market, because a Lord who overextends can be a commoner by the next monsoon.

Membership is bought with success and kept with nerve. The consortium will sponsor any promising adventurer, fund any plausible quest, and back any faction, for a price and a percentage, and it judges newcomers purely by whether their ventures pay. Individual Lords run the full range from charming philanthropists to ruthless profiteers, and the difference is rarely visible until the contract is signed.

The tradition that turns romantic is the Written-Off Debt. Every relationship among the Lords begins as an account of favors and IOUs. When one Merchant Lord quietly forgives everything another owes them (and lets them know it) they are saying the thing their whole culture forbids saying plainly: that this person is worth more than the ledger.

The argument that never closes: is the coast a market or a community? The profiteers say everything and everyone has a price the sea will pay. The philanthropists (and there are more than the reputation suggests) argue that a consortium that will sell anything eventually sells the very waters it depends on.

A playable hook: a Merchant Lord offers to write off a crushing debt the player never knowingly incurred, because someone signed the player's name to it long ago, and the Lord wants to know who.
silver-crescent-academy-culture:
## The Silver Crescent Academy: Culture and Daily Life

A day at the Silver Crescent is ranked, watched, and quietly cutthroat beneath a veneer of scholarship. The continent's premier magical academy, sitting near Aureliath, admits students on talent regardless of birth, officially, while noble families shape admissions, faculty, and curriculum from behind the arras. Class rankings are posted where everyone can see them, and they cause more interpersonal drama than most actual wars.

The hierarchy is gloriously convoluted: faculty over students on paper, but the student council president wields more real influence than most minor nobles, and a top-ranked student can bend rules a professor cannot. Alliances form around study circles, dueling societies, and the alumni network; one of Luxcellia's most powerful unofficial organizations, whose favor outlasts any grade.

Admission is talent, politics, and timing in uneven measure. A brilliant commoner and a mediocre heir may sit in the same lecture, and the Academy pretends not to notice the difference while everyone else counts it constantly. The students who thrive learn early that magic is the curriculum and leverage is the education.

The tradition that electrifies romance is the Paired Casting. Advanced students must complete a joint working with a partner of their choosing, and the choice is scrutinized ruthlessly, because a Paired Casting requires a trust the whole school can see. Choosing someone as your partner is an announcement; refusing an obvious partner is a scandal.

The argument that defines the place: is the Academy a meritocracy or a machine for laundering noble privilege into earned prestige? The idealists point at every commoner who rose on talent alone. The cynics point at the admissions ledgers and the faculty appointments and ask who really writes the rankings.

A playable hook: the player is entered into the rankings under circumstances no one will explain, placed above students who have trained for years, and given a Paired Casting partner they did not choose and cannot refuse.
legendary-arsenal-of-luxcellia:
Luxcellia's greatest weapons and armor are not sold in any shop. They are the Legendary Arsenal: named artifacts, each with a history, a resting place, and a price of entry. Adventurers trade rumors of them the way merchants trade gold.

There are three ways the Arsenal comes into a hero's hands.

First, the deep vaults. Nearly every region hides a sealed chamber at the bottom of its most dangerous dungeon, where an artifact waits behind trials, wards, or a slumbering guardian. Reaching the vault is the quest; opening it is the reward.

Second, the great beasts. Some legendaries are not stored but carried, borne by apex monsters and dungeon sovereigns that must be defeated for the artifact to fall as Riftlight. These are the rarest drops in the world, and the drop is never guaranteed on the first attempt.

Third, the earned artifacts. A few weapons answer only to a completed vow: a quest chain, a sworn oath, a debt repaid. No amount of raw strength opens these; only the story does.

Rarity holds to the world's standard tiers. Legendary items are famous and history-bearing. Mythic items are reality-bending, divine, demonic, or Reborn-linked, and only the deepest trials or the final arcs yield them. A player who carries even one piece of the Arsenal is no longer an adventurer. They are a name others tell stories about.
emberwake-dragonheart-vault: Deep beneath Kagutsuchi Emberwake, past rivers of molten rock, the Dragonheart Caldera holds a forge older than the oni clans. Its final chamber is guarded by a slumbering ember-wyrm whose scales have never cooled. Those who best it, or slip past while it dreams, may claim Zenith, the World-Severing Edge, or the Worldrender Waraxe. The Everburning Wyrmheart Focus is torn directly from the beast's chest. The heat alone has turned back armies; the guardian has turned back everyone else.
tidelace-sunken-palace-vault: Beneath the tides of Tsukihana Tidelace lies the Moon-Tide Palace Below, a drowned court that surfaces only under a full moon. Its throne room still holds the regalia of the sunken king: the Drowned Crown, the Crown Shard of the Sunken King, and the Deeptide Sovereign Trident. The sea itself tests intruders, and only those who can breathe the deep or bargain with its guardians reach the throne. The tide takes back what it is not ready to give.
twilight-obsidian-spire-vault: The Obsidian Spire pierces the sky of the Twilight Dominion, a tower of black glass where the demon court keeps its most dangerous prizes. The Abyssal Choir Rod, the Umbral Throne Regalia-Blade, and the Voidmaw Nullstaff rest at its peak, each guarded by a contract-bound sentinel that demands a price in return. Some artifacts here are won by combat; others by a bargain a wiser hero would refuse. The Spire always offers a shortcut, and the shortcut always costs.
deephollow-sealed-threshold-vault: At the lowest reach of Kurogane Deephollow, past the crystal veins, stands the Sealed Threshold: a vault-door no pick has opened, only resonance. Behind it wait the Tectonic Grand Warhammer, the Heartcrystal Resonant Blade, and the Endless Coil Chainblade, forged by dwarven smiths whose names the mountain has forgotten. A crystalsinger's true note, or a great enough deed, is the only key. The mountain does not hurry, and neither does its reward.
veilpeak-frozen-sky-vault: High in Yukishiro Veilpeak, where the air thins to knives, the Frozen Sky Gate opens onto a monastery vault sealed in unmelting ice. The Eternal Winter Scepter and the Sky-Fist of the Ascended Monk are kept here, earned only by those who climb without shelter and prove their resolve against the cold itself. The mountain's guardian is the mountain. Many who set out to claim these never return, and the peak keeps their names.
ecclesia-buried-reliquary-vault: Beneath Sanctum Ecclesia lies the Saint's Buried Reliquary, where the Church entombed relics too holy and too dangerous to display. The Sunforge Grand Staff, the Reliquary Staff of the Highest Choir, and the Mythic Aegis of the Eternal Dawn rest in consecrated silence. The reliquary opens only to the genuinely faithful or the genuinely worthy, and it can tell the difference. Presumption is turned away at the door, gently the first time.
verdania-elder-heart-vault: At the center of the Verdania Wilds grows the Elder Tree Heart, a living chamber inside the world's oldest tree. It does not hide its treasures so much as decide who may take them. The Worldroot Living Stave, the Skyfall Deadeye Bow, and the Worldtree Living Aegis are grown, not stored, and offered only to those the wild judges kind. Cruelty finds the chamber empty. Patience finds it generous.
aetherglass-fallen-observatory-vault: The Fallen Observatory drifts at the edge of the Aetherglass Reaches, a ruin of clockwork and broken sky-glass. Its artificers left behind the Kingslayer Repeater, the Crownfall Gravitic Orb, and the Foldspace Sovereign Cube, each locked behind a mechanism that must be solved rather than smashed. The Observatory rewards the clever over the strong. Force only jams the gears, and the gears remember.
crownveil-royal-vault: Within Crownveil Sovereignty, past the Royal Summoning Annex, lies the crown vault where Luxcellia's rulers kept their war-treasures. The Aegisbreaker Tower Shield, the Crown of the Undethroned, and the Duelist's Final Answer are held here under the seal of the throne. Access is a matter of standing as much as strength: earn the crown's favor, or take what the crown will not give and answer for it. Nobility opens this door; so does a very good reason.
spiritfen-dreaming-isle-vault: In the mists of Meikyo Spiritfen floats the Dreaming Isle, reachable only by those who can walk between sleep and waking. The Grave-Warden Kusarigama and the Deepdream Weaver's Loom-Rod wait within a dream that guards itself, reshaping to test the dreamer. Wake at the wrong moment and the isle is simply gone. The spirits decide who has dreamed deeply enough to deserve what the isle keeps.
guild-danger-ratings:
Every settlement, road, and dungeon in Luxcellia carries a Guild danger rating, posted on boards at every guild hall and painted on the waystones at region borders. The system exists because the Adventurers' Guild got tired of burying people who wandered somewhere they could not read.

The ratings run in six steps, and adventurers learn them before they learn to swing a sword.

SAFE (green seal). Settlements and havens. Guild-warded, patrolled, and quiet. Monsters do not enter. You may sleep, drink, court, shop, and heal here without watching the door.

LOW (white seal). Frontier country. Real danger exists but forgives mistakes. Recommended for newly registered adventurers, roughly ranks F through E.

MODERATE (blue seal). Standard adventuring ground, the bread and butter of guild work. Ranks D through C.

HIGH (bronze seal). Serious country. Parties come prepared or they do not come back. Ranks C through B.

SEVERE (silver seal). Veteran ground where the things living there are stronger than most guild members will ever be. Rank A and up.

DEADLY (black seal). The Guild does not recommend these places. It merely records who went in. Rank S, or the reckless.

The rating describes the place, not the person. A black-seal ruin does not become gentler because a novice walked in, and a white-seal road does not sprout monsters to trouble a veteran. That honesty is the whole point: the world is what it is, and you decide what to walk into.
reading-the-danger-tells:
Experienced adventurers rarely need the guild board. Luxcellia tells you where you are, if you know how to look.

THE WAYSTONES. Every regional border carries a marked stone with the seal color and a recommended rank cut into it. Guild cartographers repaint them each season. A stone scratched out usually means the rating went up and nobody wanted to be the one to write it.

THE LOCALS. Nothing tells you a place is beyond you faster than how the residents look at you. In gentle country, strangers are greeted. In severe country, a veteran will stop a newcomer at the gate and ask, plainly, whether they know where they are. Guards in deadly regions do not warn people twice.

THE DEAD. Deep country is littered with the gear of people better equipped than you. A rusted sword driven into the ground as a marker, a pack nobody came back for, a name carved into a trailhead post. Read the equipment. If it is finer than yours, turn around.

THE MONSTERS THEMSELVES. Ambient wildlife tells the honest story. If the vermin near the road are larger than the beasts you have been hunting, you have crossed a line. Creatures in high-rated country move without urgency, because nothing there needs to hurry.

THE QUIET. The most reliable tell of all. In safe country the world is noisy: birds, insects, distant voices. Deadly ground goes silent, because everything small enough to make noise has already been eaten.

A Luxcellian saying holds that the world always warns you three times before it kills you. Most people only notice the third.
the-six-attributes:
Every soul that wakes in Luxcellia is measured along six lines. Adventurers call them the Six, guild clerks call them the intake figures, and the Church calls them the shape a soul was given. They decide what comes easily to you and what you will have to fight for.

STRENGTH is force applied and force endured on your feet. It carries heavy weapons, braces a spear against a charge, breaks what will not open, and hammers steel into shape. Warriors, knights, smiths, and anyone whose answer to a problem involves leverage.

DEXTERITY is precision and speed. It draws a bow true, places a blade between ribs, moves silently across a rooftop, and does the fine handwork that turns raw material into jewelry, clothing, or a carved bow stave. Duelists, archers, rogues, and the crafts that live in the fingertips.

CONSTITUTION is endurance and the body's willingness to keep paying. It holds a shield line, survives a long delve, works a mine shift, and pays the price that blood magic demands. It is the least glamorous of the Six and the reason people come home.

INTELLIGENCE is study and structure. Nearly all elemental and arcane magic runs on it, along with alchemy, enchanting, engineering, and every craft where a formula produces a result. Mages, artificers, and scholars who believe the world can be understood.

WISDOM is perception and judgment. It reads a person's real intent, senses a crystal vein through stone, knows which mushroom kills, and hears what the divine and the spirits actually say. Priests, shrine maidens, foragers, and appraisers live here.

CHARISMA is force of self. It persuades, deceives, commands a room, and bends shadow and curse to a will that simply insists. Bards, nobles, demon-touched casters, and beast keepers whose animals obey because of who is holding the lead.

No attribute is stronger than another. A charismatic shadowcaster and a brilliant pyromancer are equally dangerous, and both will lose to the constitution-built shield saint who refuses to fall over. The Six describe how you win, not whether you do.
reading-attribute-labels:
Guild intake sheets, class charters, and skill certifications all carry the same two lines at the bottom, and new adventurers are taught to read them before anything else.

PRIMARY ATTRIBUTE is the line a discipline leans on hardest. A Swordsman's charter reads Strength because the weapon rewards leverage. A Pyromancer's reads Intelligence because fire answers formula. Raise the primary and everything in that discipline gets easier at once.

SECONDARY ATTRIBUTE appears only on hybrid disciplines, the ones that genuinely want two things. A Spellblade's charter reads Strength and Intelligence because the style is a blade and a spell in the same motion, and neglecting either half leaves you with a worse version of both. A Paladin reads Strength and Wisdom. A Gunblade Duelist reads Dexterity and Strength.

A discipline with a secondary is not weaker. It is more demanding to build and more flexible once built, which is exactly the trade the guild wants written down before a novice commits.

The practical advice every guild clerk gives: pick the discipline you actually want to play, then read its lines and put your points where they say. The sheet is not telling you who to be. It is telling you what the road will ask for.
the-mythic-six:
Six creatures in Luxcellia are not classified as monsters. The Guild lists them separately, under a heading most clerks will not read aloud, and every entry carries the same instruction: do not engage, do not pursue, report and withdraw.

They are the Mythic Six, and most scholars die without proof that any of them exist.

VAELTHYRION, THE DAWNVEIL sleeps in the deep vents beneath the Dragonheart Caldera, older than every naming convention on the continent. It hoards oaths rather than gold, and a promise sworn before it binds like law.

KORIKANE, THE ANSWERING VOICE lies coiled beneath Yukishiro Veilpeak's oldest ice. Miners have heard its bell-song rising through the glacier for as long as there have been mines. The Moonwatch has a theory about what it is answering and will not write it down.

THE MOONLIT LEVIATHAN rises only under certain moons off the Tidelace coast. The night before it surfaces, the tide-readers say the sea dreams differently, and goes glass-still for a mile.

OARASHI, SIRE OF THE STORM-HERDS is the first storm-beast and father of every thunder-hooved herd in the Duskfields. The Windrunners say the herds kneel twice: for the Sire, and for whoever the Sire has chosen.

THE VERDANT SOVEREIGN is the elder stag of deepest Verdania, antlers grown like the Elder Tree's canopy in miniature. The Verdant Throne takes its name from the legend and holds its highest ceremonies on the assumption it might attend.

THE EMBERWAKE PHOENIX nests, if it nests, in the Kagutsuchi Emberwake's living heart. Legend holds a freely-given feather returns one soul the world did not catch. The Church suppresses the rumour, the Twilight Court prices it, and the grieving would burn kingdoms for it.

Each is met only in its own territory, and the world always announces them first: an omen, a silence, a herd kneeling toward the horizon. Anyone who claims one was encountered by accident is lying, or was not paying attention to the three days before.
crafting-in-luxcellia:
Every adventurer eventually meets the same wall: the gear that carried them through the last region will not carry them through the next. In Luxcellia the answer is rarely a shop. It is a workshop.

THE TIER LADDER. Crafting materials sort into five broad tiers, and every craftsman in the world uses the same shorthand. Tier one is common stock, the iron ore and tanned hide and honest cloth that fill a frontier workshop. Tier two is uncommon: silver, direwolf pelt, mana crystal, the first materials with a personality. Tier three is rare, and this is where a craftsman's reputation begins: deepvein steel, basilisk leather, spiritwood, resonance stone. Tier four is epic, worked only by masters with proper facilities, and tier five is legendary, where a single ingot funds a house.

MATERIALS COME FROM SOMEWHERE. Nothing in a Luxcellian workshop appears from a menu. Ore is mined, hide is harvested from something that objected, herbs are foraged at the right season, monster parts are cut before the Riftlight fades, and crystal is prospected by ear. A craftsman who does not gather learns to pay someone who does, and the trade between gatherer and maker is the quiet economy holding every settlement together.

QUALITY IS NOT LUCK. The same recipe in two hands produces two different results. Material tier sets the ceiling. The craftsman's skill decides how close to that ceiling the work lands. Tools matter, workspace matters, and being rushed matters most of all. A masterwork blade and a serviceable one can leave the same forge on the same day, and the difference is entirely in who was holding the hammer.

THE GUILD RECOGNIZES FOUR GRADES. Serviceable, Fine, Masterwork, and Signature. Only the last carries the maker's mark, and only a craftsman confident enough to be found by an unhappy customer applies one.
enchanting-and-runework:
Magic can be persuaded to stay. That is the whole of enchanting, and everything else is technique.

THE VESSEL DECIDES THE CEILING. An enchantment is only as strong as the object holding it. A masterwork blade accepts and holds a working that would shatter a common one, which is why every serious enchanter keeps a smith on good terms. Enchanting a poor vessel is a slow, expensive way to make scrap.

WOVEN VERSUS APPLIED. A surface enchantment is faster, cheaper, and fades. An enchantment woven into the material during its making is permanent, far stronger, and requires the enchanter to be present at the forge or the loom. Adventurers rarely notice the difference until the day a surface working wears off mid-fight.

LAYERING. A skilled enchanter can stack multiple workings into one item without them fighting each other, but every layer strains the vessel. Two is common. Three marks a master. Four is the sort of thing that ends up with a name and a history, and the sort of thing that occasionally explodes.

RUNEWORK IS THE OTHER ROAD. Where enchanting persuades, rune carving instructs. A carved rune is a written command the world honors as long as the carving holds. Runes are more precise, more durable, and utterly unforgiving of error: a single miscut line does not weaken the working, it changes what the working says. Arrays of runes cooperating together can ward a threshold, trap a corridor, or hold a barrier for years. A Grand Seal, the highest expression of the craft, can bind something that should never be released.

THE COST. Every enchantment needs a charge. Mana crystals, riftlight shards, ley-touched filament, and for the greatest workings, something of the enchanter themselves. The Academy does not teach that last part until the fourth year.
upgrading-and-reforging:
A favorite weapon does not have to be left behind. Luxcellia's smiths have three answers for gear you have grown attached to, and all three cost something.

REFORGING rebuilds an existing item with better material, keeping its shape, balance, and name. The blade you carried out of your first dungeon can be reforged in deepvein steel and then in mythril, and it remains recognizably itself the whole way. Reforging preserves any enchantment already woven into the item and always costs more than making something new, which is exactly why people do it.

TEMPERING pushes an item past its intended limits without changing its materials. A tempered weapon hits harder and holds an edge longer, but each tempering makes the metal more brittle, and there is a point past which a smith will simply refuse. Reputable workshops mark how many temperings an item has taken. Disreputable ones do not.

AWAKENING is the rare one. Some items, usually those carried through something significant, begin to develop properties nobody put there. A blade that has taken a life it should not have. A cloak that survived a fire that killed its owner's whole party. Smiths call these living gear, and awakening is the craft of coaxing that latent property into something usable rather than something unpredictable. It cannot be forced, only recognized, and most craftsmen will only attempt it on an item they did not make.

WHAT CANNOT BE DONE. No smith can reforge a Legendary artifact. They were made by hands or forces beyond the current craft, and the honest answer every master gives is the same: I would only ruin it.
the-professions-of-luxcellia:
Not everyone who matters in Luxcellia swings a sword. The Guild recognizes dozens of professions, and the good ones are as sought-after as any A-rank.

THE MAKERS. Blacksmiths and armorsmiths keep the frontier alive. Leatherworkers, tailors, and woodworkers handle everything the smiths cannot. Jewelers set the stones that enchanters charge. Artificers and rune carvers work the line where craft becomes magic, and neither will admit the other's discipline is harder.

THE GATHERERS. Miners, foragers, herbalists, fishers, farmers, crystal prospectors, and monster harvesters supply everyone else. It is unglamorous work with a brutal failure rate at the higher tiers, and a prospector who can find a resonance vein by ear will never lack for offers.

THE PROVIDERS. Cooks, battle chefs, brewmasters, and perfumers make the difference between a party that endures a long campaign and one that falls apart in week three. A battle chef who can turn monster meat into a meal that heals is worth more on a deep delve than an extra sword.

THE DEALERS AND SPECIALISTS. Merchants, relic appraisers, treasure seekers, dungeon surveyors, and scribes. The appraiser who can tell a genuine relic from a good forgery saves fortunes. The surveyor who maps a floor correctly saves lives.

THE CIVIL TRADES. Guild receptionists, attendants, hot spring hosts, spirit mediums, musicians, actors, and playwrights. Luxcellia is not only a place to fight in. Somebody has to run the teahouse, and the person who runs the teahouse hears everything.

MASTERY IS PUBLIC. A profession advanced to its highest tier is recorded by the Guild and known by name across a region. People travel for a master's work. That reputation is its own kind of power, and it opens doors that no amount of combat rank ever will.
gathering-and-the-material-trade:
Ask a frontier smith where their iron comes from and they will name a person, not a place. Luxcellia's material trade runs on relationships.

WHERE THINGS COME FROM. Ore and gems come out of Kurogane Deephollow and the mining camps of the frontier. Hides and monster parts come from wherever the beasts are, which increasingly means wherever adventurers have been. Herbs and reagents come from Verdania and the Spiritfen, cut at the right season by people who know which season that is. Silk and thread come from the Tidelace and the deep caves. Volcanic material comes out of Emberwake at a price that reflects how many people die getting it.

THE HARVEST WINDOW. Monster materials must be cut before the Riftlight finishes dissolving the body, which is usually a matter of minutes. A harvester who arrives late gets nothing. This is why serious parties bring one, and why Monster Harvesting is quietly one of the most valuable skills a support member can carry.

SEASONS AND CYCLES. Herbs peak. Veins deplete and slowly refill. Certain fish run only under certain moons. A gatherer who understands the cycles produces several times what a stronger, faster, less patient one manages.

THE CARAVANS. The Cerulean Merchant Lords and the Windrunner Confederacy move most of the continent's material volume between them, and the rivalry is old and mostly polite. A crate of tier-three material crossing three regions accrues markup at every stop, which is precisely why adventurers who gather their own materials get so smug about it.

AND THE BLACK MARKET. Some materials cannot be traded openly. Demonheart embers, dreamspores, basilisk eyes, and anything harvested from a sapient creature move through quieter channels, and the Church takes a keen interest in who is buying.
the-lastlight-front:
## The Lastlight Front

The border war is not one war. It is three, fought across the same ground, and the ground is the approach to Lastlight Bridge, the ancient span that carries the only good road north out of the Ashenmere Frontier. Its north end comes down on Ecclesia ground at the Pilgrim's Lantern Road checkpoint, and from the Crossroads beyond it the Crown's war road runs east into the Crownveil Crownlands. The Crown garrisons both gatehouses under the Lastlight Accord, the Church's grudging leave for royal soldiers on its border.

The stakes are geographic and total. The Twilight Dominion's army, anchored at Gloamspire Camp on the frontier side, wants Lastlight intact, because whoever holds the bridge can march a real force into the Crownlands. The Crownveil Sovereignty, walled up in Fort Dawnsward on the Crown side, has reduced its entire strategy to one sentence, the fort must not fall, and justifies nearly anything by it, including bleeding its own protected villages white. The Sanctum Ecclesia fights a different war entirely from the Vigil of Saint Aurel: to the Church this is contamination, not territory, answered with quarantine and pyre rather than treaty.

Between the three grinds everyone the war forgot. Greyhaven, the first Crown village up the war road from the bridge, is officially protected and functionally abandoned, requisitioned by the fort, suspected by the Church, and raided by the Dominion. Bannerfall Field, just south of the bridge, is the killing ground where the skirmishes actually happen, and where the Frontier's Riftmaws have begun feeding on the carnage, their monsters growing coordinated in a way no one wants to be responsible for noticing.

And in the chaos, the opportunists: mercenaries and war-dogs who prey on the abandoned, deserters who sell what the dead left, and schemers like Baron Thorne who have found that military necessity is the perfect cover for turning a war's misery into a private fortune. No side on the Lastlight Front is clean. Each is sympathetic and monstrous by turns, each is certain it is the only one keeping something worse at bay, and each is, in its own way, right, which is exactly why the front does not end.
back-equipment:
# Back Equipment

The Back slot holds one cape, cloak, shawl or separate mantle alongside body armor. Only the equipped piece supplies its listed equipment bonuses; carrying spare cloaks adds no bonus. Changing backwear ends the old piece's equipped benefits and applies the new piece's benefits without losing either item.

Reborn Star Mantle and Moonwatch Vigil Mantle use Back. Voidweave Shadowmantle remains full-body protective attire in Body, as do actual coats and bark armor. A separate hood belongs in Head. Choose by the garment's construction, not the word mantle in its name.

Backwear emphasizes style, outdoor utility and modest situational protection. A cape does not confer flight, invisibility, charm or immunity unless the item explicitly defines that power and its limits. Natural wings are anatomy, not equipment. Backpacks and quivers keep their existing storage and ammunition treatment; this slot adds neither capacity nor free ammunition. Relics keep the Relic slot.

Guild Roadcloak is ordinary rainwear from guild outfitters. Frostbell Fur Cape suits cold travel. Lanternstage Half-Cape serves performers. Rosethorn Evening Shawl is formal attire. Emberglass Ashcloak suits volcanic expeditions without making its wearer fireproof. Moonlit Promise Mantle is a deliberately crafted and exchanged gift, never an automatic romance reward.

Tailors and outfitters sell or commission appropriate pieces. Use actual materials, agreed prices, crafting effort and an on-screen acquisition. Armor loot can include backwear without adding extra drops. No character is automatically given a cape by this update.
adventurer-companies:
Adventurer Companies are bands of adventurers chartered under the Adventurer's Guild, the way a trading house is chartered under a city. Every guild hall keeps a Company Board beside its contract boards: each Company's crest, rank, and the hall it calls home. Individual adventurers keep their own F to S rank; a Company earns a separate standing of its own.

Founding a Company: a founder and at least two willing partners register it at any Adventurer's Guild hall. Registration needs a name no other Company holds, a crest the clerks can paint on the board, the charter fee of one Gold Coin, and an address. The address can be a rented inn room at first; a real hall comes later through the ordinary property market. Partners must agree in the scene; nobody is signed onto a charter by assumption. The founder answers to the Guild for the charter, and the founder chooses the name and crest.

Company ranks: Iron, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Mythril. New Companies start at Iron. Rank rises from contracts finished under the banner, not from members' personal ranks, so a Company of B-rank veterans is still Iron until it proves itself together. Roughly: Bronze after a handful of Company Contracts, Silver after a truly dangerous one, Gold for deeds a whole region talks about, and Mythril only by Guild decision. Gold Companies are famous in their region. Mythril Companies are known across the continent, and only one flies a Mythril banner today: Stormblood Vanguard, which invites its members and never offers trials.

Company Contracts: some work is posted only to Companies: long escorts, multi-floor dungeon surveys, region-wide hunts, and dives that need more hands than one party. Contract pay goes to the Company and follows the Guild's normal pay bands for the danger; how it is split is the Company's business.

The Riftmaw Depth Board: at the Floor Zero Gatehouse, the Guild keeps a board of the deepest floor each Company has reached and come back from. The Deepwatch Lantern Company has held the top line for years. Stormblood Vanguard never posts its dives, and nobody outside it knows how deep it has been.

Joining a Company: Companies recruit by trial. Ask a member, take one trial contract alongside them, and the leader decides. Membership means a crest pin, a standing welcome at the hall, a share of Company work, and people who will come for you in a real emergency. It is not a party: Company-mates keep their own posts and lives and travel with a member only when they agree to, scene by scene. An adventurer flies one Company's banner at a time and may leave to join another or found their own.

Rivalry: Companies compete for contracts, recruits, and the Depth Board. Rivals poach members, undercut bids, and race each other to the same bounty, but open violence between chartered Companies costs both their charters. Unchartered bands that call themselves companies exist too, mercenaries mostly, and the Guild owes them nothing.

Known Companies: Stormblood Vanguard (Mythril, Abyssal-floor expeditions), Deepwatch Lantern Company (Gold, Riftmaw dives), The Flagon Irregulars (Silver, monster bounties), Tidecrest Company (Silver, coastal escorts), The Gilded Caravan Company (Gold, desert caravans), The Frostfang Hunt (Silver, mountain hunts), The Greenwake Company (Gold, forest trails), The Vaunted Blade Company (Gold, tournaments), The Emberforge Company (Silver, ore runs). Many smaller Companies exist; once one is named in a story, its name, crest, rank, members, and hall stay the same.
